challenges.name: harden-vibe-coded-app-evidence
challenges.title: Harden the Vibe-Coded App: read the evidence
challenges.description: Instructor Binh edited a course that belongs to instructor Ana through the vibe-coded course studio API, and one of his requests moved another of Ana's courses to him. Six statements on one evidence pack - the access log and the courses table (A), the handler (B), the agent conversation (C) and the agent's tests (D) - take you from reading the evidence to a hypothesis, past two wrong explanations, to the fix and its verification.

questions.question:
Evidence A - API access log (api.codedev.test) and the courses table afterwards:
2026-10-19T08:58:02Z POST  /api/auth/login        200 user=u_binh role=instructor sess=s_91c4 ip=198.51.100.7 ua=Firefox/131
2026-10-19T09:02:11Z PATCH /api/courses/c_101     200 user=u_ana  role=instructor sess=s_7f2a ip=203.0.113.24 ua=Chrome/130 keys=title,price
2026-10-19T09:12:40Z PATCH /api/courses/c_101     200 user=u_binh role=instructor sess=s_91c4 ip=198.51.100.7 ua=curl/8.5.0 keys=title
2026-10-19T09:14:03Z PATCH /api/courses/c_102     200 user=u_binh role=instructor sess=s_91c4 ip=198.51.100.7 ua=curl/8.5.0 keys=ownerId,title
2026-10-19T09:30:55Z GET   /api/studio/my-courses 200 user=u_ana  role=instructor sess=s_7f2a ip=203.0.113.24 ua=Chrome/130 count=1

 id    | owner_id | title
 c_101 | u_ana    | Binh was here
 c_102 | u_binh   | Indexes (test)

Statement: "Binh changed the title of Ana's course c_101 with his own session, and his request to c_102 with the keys ownerId and title moved that course to him, which is why Ana's dashboard now shows one course."
questions.explanation: True. Every PATCH from Binh carries user=u_binh and sess=s_91c4, the session created by his own login at 08:58 from his own IP, and both answered 200. The table shows c_101 still owned by u_ana but with Binh's title, and c_102 now owned by u_binh: the request with keys=ownerId,title rewrote the owner. Ana's "my courses" query (count=1) lists courses by owner_id, so c_102 left her dashboard. Reading the evidence line by line first keeps you from fixing the wrong thing: this is not a lost course or a display bug, it is a write the API accepted.

True. B answers "who are you?" (authentication) and "what kind of user are you?" (the role), but never "is this object yours?" - the missing object-level authorization that the OWASP API Security Top 10 lists first, as Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA). Passing the whole body to the update is the property-level version of the same problem (mass assignment): every column, ownerId included, becomes writable. C shows the agent did what it was asked: "only instructors can edit" was the whole requirement, and its summary even says the body is passed through. The common misconception is that the agent disobeyed; the requirement was incomplete, and the person who merged it owns that gap.

questions.question:
Evidence A - API access log (api.codedev.test) and the courses table afterwards:
2026-10-19T08:58:02Z POST  /api/auth/login        200 user=u_binh role=instructor sess=s_91c4 ip=198.51.100.7 ua=Firefox/131
2026-10-19T09:02:11Z PATCH /api/courses/c_101     200 user=u_ana  role=instructor sess=s_7f2a ip=203.0.113.24 ua=Chrome/130 keys=title,price
2026-10-19T09:12:40Z PATCH /api/courses/c_101     200 user=u_binh role=instructor sess=s_91c4 ip=198.51.100.7 ua=curl/8.5.0 keys=title
2026-10-19T09:14:03Z PATCH /api/courses/c_102     200 user=u_binh role=instructor sess=s_91c4 ip=198.51.100.7 ua=curl/8.5.0 keys=ownerId,title
2026-10-19T09:30:55Z GET   /api/studio/my-courses 200 user=u_ana  role=instructor sess=s_7f2a ip=203.0.113.24 ua=Chrome/130 count=1

 id    | owner_id | title
 c_101 | u_ana    | Binh was here
 c_102 | u_binh   | Indexes (test)

Statement: "Ana's session was hijacked: the edits were made with a stolen session, so invalidating every session and forcing a new login closes the hole."
questions.explanation: False. The edits came from s_91c4, which belongs to u_binh: it was created by his own login at 08:58 from 198.51.100.7, and every PATCH from it is logged as user=u_binh. Ana's session s_7f2a was only used from her own IP and browser. Invalidating sessions changes nothing: Binh logs in again with his own valid account and the same request works, because the API lets any instructor edit any course. The misconception is to reach for the scariest explanation (a stolen session) before reading the user and session fields in the log.

False. The log shows role=instructor on every one of Binh's requests, and B lets any instructor through: the role check worked exactly as written, and any other instructor could do the same thing tomorrow. A role answers "may this kind of user edit courses at all?"; it cannot answer "may this user edit this course?", which needs the course's owner_id compared with the caller's id. The misconception is to treat an object-level question as a role (RBAC) problem.

False. Binh's two PATCH requests were sent with ua=curl/8.5.0, not from the studio: anyone with a valid session can call the API directly, with any course id and any body. The UI is a convenience, not a security boundary. The fix belongs in the handler: compare the course owner with the caller (admins excepted, with one documented answer such as 404 for "missing or not yours"), and accept only an allowlist of editable fields so that ownerId, id and createdAt can never be set through PATCH. Hiding the button is still good UX, as an addition to the server check.

True. Every test in D has a single user: the owner on the happy path, then an anonymous user and a learner, whom the session and role checks already reject. No test has two instructors, so the missing owner check is invisible to the suite: it is green because it never asks the question. A test with Ana and Binh fails today (B returns 200 and the title changes) and passes once the handler compares owner_id with the caller. Add one with ownerId in the body and one with an admin, and the suite pins the whole policy. The misconception is that passing tests written by the same agent prove the requirement is safe; they prove only what they check.

challenges.name: spot-the-ai-mistake-admin-api-owner-check
challenges.title: Spot the AI Mistake: an admin API without an owner check
challenges.description: The CodeDev course studio was vibe-coded in a weekend. The request sent to the coding agent was: "Add an edit endpoint for courses in the course studio. Only instructors can edit. Keep it simple, the demo is on Monday." Its handler updateCourse (PATCH /api/courses/:id, plain TypeScript with an in-memory store and sessions that the auth middleware has already resolved) passes the agent's tests, but on Monday instructor Binh edited a course owned by instructor Ana, and a request from Binh with "ownerId" in the body moved another of Ana's courses to him. Fix updateCourse so that it follows this policy, checked in this order: (1) no user (missing or unknown session): 401 {"error":"unauthenticated"}; (2) a role other than instructor or admin: 403 {"error":"forbidden"}; (3) a body that is not a JSON object (null, an array, a string): 400 {"error":"invalid_body"}; (4) the course does not exist, or the caller is an instructor who does not own it (course.ownerId differs from user.id): 404 {"error":"not_found"}, the same answer in both cases so that the API does not reveal which course ids exist; an admin may edit any course; (5) the body keys, in their order: a key other than title, description and price (id, ownerId, createdAt or any unknown field) gives 400 {"error":"field_not_editable","field":<key>}; an invalid value gives 400 {"error":"invalid_field","field":<key>} (title: a string that is not blank, description: a string, price: an integer >= 0); the first failing key decides; (6) otherwise 200 with the updated course, in which only the keys of the body changed. A rejected request changes nothing, and nobody can change ownerId through this endpoint, not even an admin. The test runner sends a list of requests, prints one line per request (status and error) and then every course in the store. The public tests pass on the agent's code; the hidden tests use a second instructor, ownerId in the body, a missing course and an admin.
hints: The agent's code asks two questions about the caller: is there a session, and is the role instructor or admin? Which question about this particular course does it never ask, and which keys of the body can end up in the stored course?

Look at the lines between `courses.get(req.params.id)` and the spread `{ ...course, ...changes }`. Which field of the course says whose it is, and what does the loop over the body do with a key it does not recognise?

A similar case on another resource: announcements { id, authorId, text, pinned }. `const a = store.get(id); if (!a || (user.role !== "admin" && a.authorId !== user.id)) return { status: 404 };` treats "missing" and "not yours" the same. For PATCH, a list of allowed keys such as `new Set(["text"])` rejects `authorId` and `pinned` before anything is copied.
